entries.topicDescription: Threads, the executor framework, and the memory-visibility rules that make concurrent code correct.

tips.title: Prefer ExecutorService over creating raw Threads
tips.content:
Creating a new Thread per task is expensive (each one owns a
full OS-level stack, typically ~1MB by default) and gives you
no control over how many run concurrently — nothing stops a
burst of work from spawning thousands of threads and starving
the system.

ExecutorService decouples "submitting work" from "how it runs":
a fixed thread pool reuses a bounded set of worker threads,
queuing tasks past that limit instead of creating new OS
threads. Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) or (since Java 21)
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() for lightweight
virtual threads are the standard starting points.

Always shut an ExecutorService down (shutdown() or, better,
try-with-resources on the AutoCloseable ExecutorService
interface added in Java 19+) — a leaked pool keeps its threads
alive and the JVM from exiting.

tips.title: synchronized guarantees both mutual exclusion AND visibility
tips.content:
It's easy to think of 'synchronized' as only preventing two
threads from running a block at the same time, but it also
solves a separate, subtler problem: memory visibility. Without
synchronization, one thread's write to a shared variable is
not guaranteed to ever become visible to another thread — each
CPU core may cache the value locally.

Entering a synchronized block establishes a "happens-before"
relationship: every write made before releasing a lock is
guaranteed visible to any thread that subsequently acquires
that same lock. Two threads synchronizing on different objects
get no such guarantee between each other.

The 'volatile' keyword provides the visibility guarantee alone,
without mutual exclusion — appropriate for a simple flag
written by one thread and read by others, but not for
compound operations like incrementing a counter (read-then-write
isn't atomic even if the field is volatile).

tips.title: java.util.concurrent's atomic classes avoid locking for simple counters
tips.content:
AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, and AtomicReference use hardware
compare-and-swap (CAS) instructions instead of locks to make
single-variable read-modify-write operations atomic —
incrementAndGet(), compareAndSet(), updateAndGet() — without
the overhead of acquiring a monitor.

CAS works by reading the current value, computing a new one,
then atomically swapping only if the value hasn't changed
since the read; if another thread beat it to the update, it
retries. This is typically faster than synchronized under
moderate contention because it never blocks a thread — it
just spins and retries.

Atomics only make a SINGLE variable's updates atomic — they
don't help coordinate multiple related fields that need to
change together consistently; that still needs a lock or a
higher-level structure like ConcurrentHashMap's atomic compute
methods.
